rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mursalāt and the preceding Sūrah al-Dahr address the same subject, but make their arguments on different bases.
rows.anchor: Though the subject of both sūrahs is the same, the nature of arguments is different.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Dahr grounds reward and punishment in human nature's awareness of good and evil; deniers are warned, while those who heed that inner testimony receive glad tidings.
rows.anchor: the awareness of good and evil ordained in human nature substantiates reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūrah bases its argument on signs in the world around people; any appeal to human nature is only rudimentary.
rows.anchor: the signs in the world around man are the basis of the arguments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the preceding sūrah is dominated by glad tidings, this one is dominated by warnings, a mood reflected in its repeated refrain.
rows.anchor: Glad tidings dominate the latter while warnings dominate this sūrah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The varied effects of winds show that the threatened punishment in this world and the Hereafter is possible.
rows.anchor: the punishment of this world and the Hereafter of which people are being warned is not something impossible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God used winds and clouds to punish earlier nations and can use these forces against the Quraysh as well.
rows.anchor: He used His winds and clouds to punish previous nations and whenever He wants He will punish the Quraysh too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People should learn from the signs of God's boons and harms; their deeds leave them no grounds to demand that punishment be hastened.
rows.anchor: If they want to thrive, they should seek a lesson from the signs which signify the boons and banes of the Almighty. They do not dare hasten it because of their deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the universe's grandest objects are mortal and dependent: everything exists by God's decree and moves only with His permission.
rows.anchor: nothing can exist of its own accord and nothing is independent; everything exists because of God’s decree and moves with His permission only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgement will present the accounts of messengers and their peoples, assessing what the messengers said and how their peoples responded; those who rejected them will be devastated.
rows.anchor: the accounts of the messengers and their people will be presented

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh are directed to their history: God destroyed earlier nations and those who followed them, showing that His treatment of criminals will not change.
rows.anchor: The Quraysh are asked to seek a lesson from their history by asking them about it; The Almighty destroyed previous nations and the succeeding ones too who followed their ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human physical structure and stages of creation display God's power, providence, and wisdom; the Creator can readily recreate people, so resurrection is certain and its deniers doomed.
rows.anchor: The purpose of this mention is that man’s own creation bears testimony that re-creating him is not at all difficult for His Creator.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth gathers the living and dead and supplies sustenance; no one escapes God's control or can do without His provision, testifying that He will gather everyone.
rows.anchor: Neither is anyone beyond God’s control nor is anyone self-sufficient from His sustenance.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who denied God's providence and power while absorbed in worldly pleasures will be cursed on the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: they while remaining inebriated by the pleasures of life kept on denying the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses portray the torment disbelievers will face in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: A portrayal of the torment that these disbelievers will face in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses depict the helplessness of the disbelievers.
rows.anchor: A depiction of the helplessness of the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These verses portray the success of those who feared God.
rows.anchor: A portrayal of the success attained by those who were fearful of the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage warns the arrogant Quraysh and expresses hopelessness that they will embrace faith.
rows.anchor: A declaration of warning to the Quraysh on their arrogance and an expression of hopelessness on their embracing faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-mursalāt means things let loose; here it refers to winds.
rows.anchor: means “those which are let loose.” Here it is used to signify winds.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some interpreters take al-mursalāt to mean angels, but Islahi rejects this because the later attributes do not suit angels.
rows.anchor: some people interpret it to signify angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The premise that oaths are always sworn by sacred beings is mistaken; Qur'anic oaths generally substantiate a claim.
rows.anchor: the basis of this erroneous interpretation is that an oath is sworn here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As with the wind oaths in Sūrah al-Dhāriyāt, this oath establishes that worldly and afterlife punishment will come if disbelievers persist in denial.
rows.anchor: oaths have been sworn by winds to substantiate reward and punishment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ʿurf is used for a horse's forelock or mane hanging over its forehead, a familiar usage illustrated by Imru’ al-Qays.
rows.anchor: comes for a horse’s mane which hangs from the forehead. It is very commonly used in this meaning. Imru’ al-Qays has said:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The horse's mane can be used to stop it or signal release; comparing winds to a horse being let loose subtly shows that they act only under God's control.
rows.anchor: A horse’s mane is used both to stop it and to give it a signal to cut loose. In this verse, winds are compared to horses and letting them loose signifies letting loose their mane.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAṣf means blowing all over in an uncontrolled manner.
rows.anchor: means “to blow all over in an uncontrolled manner.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The raging tempest and engulfing waves described at 10:22 illustrate the violent, uncontrolled wind meant here.
rows.anchor: a raging tempest overtakes them and waves embrace them from all sides

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the second phase: after release, winds blow without restraint as destructive tempests that can devastate whole nations, an effect recorded in revelation and still observable.
rows.anchor: This is the second phase in which after being let loose, winds blow in an unrestrained manner. This obviously refers to tempestuous winds which become a torment and destroy complete nations.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nashr can mean scattering, sprinkling, bringing forth, or causing growth; the Qur'an uses it in all these senses.
rows.anchor: to scatter, to sprinkle, to bring forth and to cause to grow.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the winds bring and scatter clouds, spread rain as God's mercy, and make vegetation grow, rendering the earth luxuriant.
rows.anchor: then sprinkle God’s mercy and then cause vegetation to grow

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding oath concerns tempestuous winds, while this oath concerns winds bringing merciful clouds on which life and nourishment depend.
rows.anchor: the previous oath relates to tempestuous winds, while this one relates to winds which bring clouds of mercy on which is dependent the existence and nourishment of various life forms.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fa joining al-ʿāṣifāt to al-mursalāt signals that the wind actions occur in sequential order.
rows.anchor: signifies sequential order. This verse is co-ordinated with the previous one

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw joining the next oath marks an independent category of winds, not a third phase in the sequence.
rows.anchor: it does not refer to a third phase in the sequence; it rather refers to an independent new category of winds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As in 51:4, the winds distribute affairs differently: they bring or disperse clouds and send abundant rain to some places while leaving others dry.
rows.anchor: they cause abundant rain from these clouds and leave another place dry and desolate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrasts in what winds do show that they are not independent but are subject to a superior power.
rows.anchor: This bears testimony to the fact that they are not independent in their actions; they are subservient to some superior power.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because this differentiation by winds follows their scattering of clouds, the coordinating particle is fa.
rows.anchor: the co-ordinated particle is ف .

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Besides bringing rain, winds instil a reminder in people.
rows.anchor: The implication is that besides rain, the winds also instil a reminder in people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain's harmony between sky and earth reminds people of God's oneness and calls them to gratitude.
rows.anchor: With respect to the harmony between the sky and the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majesty of God's providence displayed in rain reminds people that they are accountable to Him.
rows.anchor: the majesty of God’s providence found in rain reminds us of our accountability to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain bringing dead, barren land to life reminds people that God will raise the dead in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: By enlivening dead and desolate pieces of land, rain reminds us of raising the dead to life in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rain's mercy for some and misery for others reminds people of God's absolute authority and His reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: By bringing mercy to some and misery to some, rain reminds us of God’s absolute authority and His reward and punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle aw (“or”) means the effects of the winds leave the indifferent without an excuse while offering those open to a reminder the chance to receive one.
rows.anchor: So that we may be free from blame in the sight of your Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿrāf 7:164 offers a parallel: the righteous explain that counselling is meant to clear their own blame before God and perhaps lead the people to fear Him.
rows.anchor: So that we may be free from blame in the sight of your Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If people reject the righteous' counsel, the counsellors have fulfilled their duty and the rejecters have no excuse at Judgement; if people heed it, fear of God benefits both.
rows.anchor: they are left with no excuse which they can present on the Day of Judgement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing oath-affirmation completes the preceding oaths; the general promise includes both promise and threat, but the warning context makes threat dominant and its punishment certain.
rows.anchor: This is the complement of all the oaths mentioned earlier.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The effects of winds warn rejecters not to boast of their power: God needs little to punish a people, and the same rain that gives life can devastate them; many nations were ravaged by winds.
rows.anchor: The same rain which brings life to people can cause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At Judgement, the universe's apparently grand, enduring, firm objects will be wrecked: stars vanish, the sky splits, and mountains crumble to dust.
rows.anchor: every object of this universe which appears very grand and great, immortal and abiding, firm and solid will be wrecked.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭams means to erase and obliterate something.
rows.anchor: means “to erase something and obliterate something.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic wording about obliterating is echoed in the warning about faces being erased and turned backward at 4:47.
rows.anchor: before We obliterate faces and turn them backwards

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other descriptions say the stars are scattered or fall away, paralleling their dimming here.
rows.anchor: At other places, the words are:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky, now whole with no fissures or crevices, will split open at Judgement, as also described at 78:19 and 82:1.
rows.anchor: the sky which has no fissures and crevices and is absolutely sound and solid will be cleft asunder on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nasf means crushing something to pieces, mashing it, and scattering it.
rows.anchor: means “to crush to pieces, to mash and to scatter.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'an 20:97 describes a worshipped idol being burned to ashes and scattered, illustrating nasf.
rows.anchor: For example, it is said:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In answer to the question about mountains, 20:105–106 says God will grind them to fine dust and leave the earth clean and level.
rows.anchor: they ask you about the mountains. Tell [them]: “My Lord will crush them to fine dust and leave the earth absolutely clean,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the mountains are described as reduced to sand dunes and appearing like a mirage.
rows.anchor: on the Day of Judgement, the mountains will be reduced to sand dunes and will appear like a mirage.
